question.text: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of increasing weakness of his right arm and leg that began when he woke up that morning. He did not notice any weakness when he went to bed the night before. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide and atorvastatin. He is alert and oriented to person, time, place. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 91/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. Examination shows drooping of the right side of the face. Muscle strength is decreased in the right upper and lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ on the right side. Sensation is intact. His speech is normal in rate and rhythm. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An infarction of which of the following sites is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.A: Posterior limb of the left internal capsule

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with unilateral weakness (right arm and leg) and facial droop, suggesting a lesion in the contralateral motor pathway. The key finding is the 4+ deep tendon reflexes on the right side, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion. The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, which are responsible for motor function. A lesion in this area would cause contralateral weakness and facial droop.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: 4+ deep tendon reflexes on the right side, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: B: Base of the left pons - While a pontine lesion could cause contralateral weakness, it would more likely involve other cranial nerve deficits (e.g., facial weakness, gaze palsies) and possibly sensory changes. C: Left posterolateral thalamus - Thalamic lesions typically cause sensory deficits, not primarily motor weakness. D: Left lateral medulla - Lateral medullary lesions typically cause Wallenberg syndrome, which involves vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner's syndrome, and loss of pain/temperature sensation on the ipsilateral face and contralateral body. E: Left cerebellar vermis - Vermis lesions typically cause truncal ataxia and gait instability, not focal weakness.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with right-sided weakness, drooping face, and increased deep tendon reflexes. These findings suggest a lesion in the corticobulbar tracts, which descend from the brainstem to the spinal cord. The posterior limb of the internal capsule is part of the corticobulbar tract and would cause right-sided weakness and reflexes. The other options (base of the pons, posterolateral thalamus, lateral medulla, cerebellar vermis) are less likely given the absence of ataxia, dysarthria, or nystagmus.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Drooping of the right side of the face and increased deep tendon reflexes on the right side
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered stroke, transverse myelitis, and MS, but ruled out due to intact sensation and normal speech. Ataxia or dysarthria would have supported a cerebellar or brainstem lesion, but these were absent.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with acute unilateral motor deficit (right arm and leg) and facial droop, consistent with a left hemisphere stroke. The absence of sensory loss and preserved speech suggests a motor pathway lesion. The 4+ deep tendon reflexes on the right indicate upper motor neuron involvement, which is typical of internal capsule or cortical stroke. The posterior limb of the internal capsule is a common site for motor stroke and explains the contralateral hemiparesis and facial droop.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Contralateral hemiparesis with facial droop and hyperreflexia strongly localize to a left posterior limb of the internal capsule lesion.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Base of the pons (B) would cause cranial nerve deficits and ataxia; thalamus (C) would cause sensory deficits; medulla (D) would cause dysphagia or Horner’s; cerebellar vermis (E) would cause truncal ataxia. All are less likely given the pure motor presentation with preserved sensation and speech.

openbio_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with acute-onset weakness of the right upper and lower extremities, along with drooping of the right side of the face. These findings are highly suggestive of a cerebrovascular accident (stroke). Given the patient's risk factors of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, the most likely location of the stroke is the posterior limb of the left internal capsule, which is a common site for lacunar infarcts in patients with these risk factors. The intact sensation and normal speech rate and rhythm help to localize the lesion to the internal capsule rather than other areas that could affect these functions.
openbio_8b.critical_evidence: The acute-onset weakness of the right upper and lower extremities and the drooping of the right side of the face.
openbio_8b.differential_considered: The most likely differential diagnosis for this patient's symptoms is a cerebrovascular accident (stroke). Other possibilities such as Bell's palsy, myasthenia gravis, or a spinal cord injury were considered but ruled out due to the absence of other neurological deficits, the acute onset of symptoms, and the specific pattern of weakness and facial droop.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other possibilities such as the left posterolateral thalamus (C), left pons (B), or cerebellar hemisphere (E) could cause motor or sensory deficits, but the specific combination of right-sided weakness and facial droop without sensory loss or ataxia points away from the thalamus or cerebellum and toward a cortical or subcortical motor structure. The absence of speech or sensory deficits also makes the lateral medulla (D) less likely, as it primarily affects sensory tracts. The findings are most consistent with a right-sided cortical or subcortical motor lesion, such as the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
